question.prompt:
Suppose \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are positive integers such that

\[ \frac{a}{14}+\frac{b}{15}=\frac{c}{210}. \]

Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

I. If \(\gcd(a,14)=1\) or \(\gcd(b,15)=1\) or both, then \(\gcd(c,210)=1.\)

II. If \(\gcd(c,210)=1,\) then \(\gcd(a,14)=1\) or \(\gcd(b,15)=1\) or both.

III. \(\gcd(c,210)=1\) if and only if \(\gcd(a,14)=\gcd(b,15)=1.\)

solutions.title: Test each prime divisor
solutions.explanation:
Only the primes \(2,3,5,7\) can give \(c\) a common factor with \(210\), so we can test these four primes individually.

Multiplying the given equation by \(210\) gives
\[
c=15a+14b,
\qquad 210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7.
\]
We reduce the equation modulo each prime. The notation \(x\equiv y\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(x-y\).

| Prime \(p\) | Congruence | Equivalent condition for \(p\mid c\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(2\) | \(c\equiv a\pmod2\) | \(2\mid a\) |
| \(3\) | \(c\equiv2b\pmod3\) | \(3\mid b\) |
| \(5\) | \(c\equiv4b\pmod5\) | \(5\mid b\) |
| \(7\) | \(c\equiv a\pmod7\) | \(7\mid a\) |

In the middle two rows, the multipliers \(2\) and \(4\) cannot supply a factor of \(3\) and \(5\), respectively. Thus those divisibility tests depend only on \(b\).

A common divisor greater than \(1\) must have a prime factor. Therefore \(c\) is relatively prime to \(210\) exactly when it avoids all four primes in the table. This happens exactly when \(a\) avoids \(2\) and \(7\), and \(b\) avoids \(3\) and \(5\). Equivalently,
\[
\gcd(c,210)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gcd(a,14)=\gcd(b,15)=1.
\]
This proves III. It also proves II, because if both gcds equal \(1\), then at least one equals \(1\).

For I, choose \(a=1\) and \(b=3\), giving \(c=15+42=57\). Although \(\gcd(a,14)=1\), we have \(\gcd(57,210)=3\). Thus I is false.

The necessarily true statements are \(\boxed{\text{II and III only}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

solutions.title: Relate the gcds directly
solutions.explanation:
Adding or subtracting a multiple of a number preserves common divisors with that number. Applying this observation to \(14\) and \(15\) relates the three gcds directly.

Clearing denominators and regrouping gives
\[
c=15a+14b=a+14(a+b)=15(a+b)-b.
\]
Any divisor of \(14\) divides \(c\) exactly when it divides \(a\), since \(c-a\) is a multiple of \(14\). Similarly, any divisor of \(15\) divides \(c\) exactly when it divides \(b\), since \(c+b\) is a multiple of \(15\). Hence
\[
\gcd(c,14)=\gcd(a,14),
\qquad
\gcd(c,15)=\gcd(b,15).
\]
Because \(14\) and \(15\) have no common prime factor, the prime factors common to \(c\) and \(210=14\cdot15\) split between these two gcds. Consequently,
\[
\gcd(c,210)
=\gcd(c,14)\gcd(c,15)
=\gcd(a,14)\gcd(b,15).
\]
The two factors on the right are positive integers, so their product equals \(1\) if and only if both equal \(1\). This proves III. It also proves II: if \(\gcd(c,210)=1\), both of the other gcds are \(1\), so at least one is \(1\).

Statement I assumes only that at least one factor equals \(1\), which need not make the product \(1\). For example, take \(a=2\) and \(b=1\), so \(c=44\). Then \(\gcd(b,15)=1\), but \(\gcd(c,210)=2\), disproving I.

Thus \(\boxed{\text{II and III only}}\) are necessarily true, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
